content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Advanced Content Management

Advanced Content Management

Control what packages and errata are published, distribute custom content, and promote versions safely through lifecycle environments.

In this lesson
Filter content by package, errata type, and module stream. Manage errata with intent. Add custom RPMs and images. Version and promote safely.
Why it matters
Uncontrolled enhancements or wrong package versions can introduce instability. Filtering and staged promotion protect production systems while still allowing fast security response.
Explore Key Topics
Filtering
Package, errata, and module stream filters to curate content sets.
Custom Content
Upload RPMs, ISOs, and push container images into Satellite's registry for internal distribution.
Promotion
Publish immutable Content View versions and promote sequentially across environments.
Concept map
Curate → Verify → Promote
Curate
Filters select which packages, errata types, and module streams are part of a Content View before publishing.
Package filters
Errata filters
Module streams
Custom repos
Verify
Publish immutable versions, test in lower environments, and apply errata selectively to hosts.
Publish CV version
Promote to Dev → QA → Prod
Promote
Sequential promotion keeps production stable and auditable. Automate with hammer or API for repeatability.
Naming & descriptions
Automation hooks

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives target the skills you'll use immediately when operating Satellite. First, you'll implement advanced Content View filters that select packages by name, version, errata type, or module stream so only approved content reaches each lifecycle stage. Second, you'll manage errata intentionally: prioritize security and bugfix updates, defer enhancements, and apply updates to hosts or host groups with minimal disruption. Third, you'll integrate custom content—uploading RPMs and ISOs and pushing container images to Satellite's registry—so internal artifacts are distributed securely. Fourth, you'll author and publish immutable Content View versions and promote them through a controlled lifecycle while troubleshooting common synchronization issues. Each objective connects to real tasks: creating a filter with hammer, applying a targeted erratum to a host, uploading an internal RPM repository, and diagnosing why a client does not see a published version. These skills reduce risk, increase reproducibility, and make audits simpler. Practice in a Development environment before applying to Production, and use the verified competency milestones to measure readiness.

screens.title: Content View Filters — What and Why
screens.narratorSegment: A Content View filter is a rule set that narrows the content included in a Content View before publishing. Filters can target package names and versions, errata types or IDs, and module streams. The core idea is curation: decide ahead of publishing what is eligible for testing and promotion. For example, if a particular package version causes instability, you can create a package filter that excludes that version so it never reaches your environments. Or, if your policy requires only security and bugfix updates in production, an errata filter that includes only those types enforces that rule consistently. A common misconception is that filters are reversible on a published version. They are not: filters affect what is included when you publish. Changing filters requires publishing a new Content View version. A concrete example: use hammer to create an errata filter named "Security_Bugfix_Only" and include only the security and bugfix types. After publishing, promote that version through your lifecycle. The key takeaway is that filters are preventive controls that enforce policy at publish time; treat them as part of your pipeline, test in lower environments, and document each filter's purpose with clear names and descriptions.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Filters selectively include or exclude packages, errata, and module streams when publishing a Content View to enforce policy and stability.

content.html:
Module 8 › Content View Filters
What is a filter?
A curated rule that decides which repository artifacts and errata are included when a Content View is published. Use them to enforce compliance and avoid problematic versions.
When to use
  • Exclude a package version that causes failures.
  • Include only security and bugfix errata in production views.
  • Enable a specific module stream for consistency across hosts.
Key takeaway
Filters are preventive: they change the published content set and require a new Content View version to take effect.
Example
hammer content-view filter create --content-view "RHEL8_Base_CV" \
  --name "Security_Bugfix_Only" \
  --type erratum \
  --inclusion-type include \
  --errata-type security,bugfix
After creating this filter, publish a new Content View version so the rule is applied.
Misconception
Changing a filter does not alter previously published versions. Treat each published version as immutable.
Key Takeaway

Design filters before publishing, name them clearly, and publish a new immutable Content View version to apply them.

screens.title: Package Name and Version Filters
screens.narratorSegment: Filtering by package name and version is a precise way to prevent a known-bad RPM from entering your lifecycle. Define an exclusion filter specifying both the package name and the offending version. This is often used when a vendor update regresses functionality or when compliance requires a fixed package version. A practical example: you discover that bad-package version 1.0.0 causes a service crash on all controllers. Create a Content View filter that excludes package "bad-package" version "1.0.0" and attach it to the Content View containing your RHEL 8 repositories. Remember filters are evaluated before publishing, so after creating the filter you must publish a new Content View version and promote it. A common mistake is excluding too broadly, for example excluding a package by name without scoping the version, which may block required updates. Another pitfall is not documenting the filter rationale. In practice, include the filter name and description that reference the bug tracking ID or incident number. The takeaway: prefer targeted exclusions, publish new versions, and test in Development before promoting to Production. Package Name and Version Filters means target package name plus version to exclude known-bad rpms while preserving healthy updates.. In practical terms, precise exclusion or inclusion of problematic rpms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Package filters
keyIdea.text: Target package name plus version to exclude known-bad RPMs while preserving healthy updates.

content.html:
Core Concept › Package Version Filters
Why filter by version?
To block a specific problematic release while allowing other versions of the same package to flow through updates.
Common mistake
Excluding by name only can prevent necessary fixes. Scope filters to versions when possible and document why the version is excluded.
Key Takeaway

Use versioned exclusions for precision, publish a new CV version, and test the result in a non-production lifecycle environment.

Example CLI
# Exclude a specific package version
hammer content-view filter create --content-view "RHEL8_Base_CV" \
  --name "Exclude_Bad_Package" \
  --type package \
  --inclusion-type exclude \
  --package-name "bad-package" \
  --package-version "1.0.0"
After running this command, publish a new Content View version to apply it.
Analogy
Think of a package filter like a safety gate that blocks a specific defective serial-number batch while leaving the rest of the production line running.

screens.title: Errata Types and Errata Filters
screens.narratorSegment: Errata in Satellite are categorized as security, bugfix, or enhancement. Each type represents different risk and priority. Security errata fix vulnerabilities and should be prioritized for most environments. Bugfix errata correct defects and typically improve stability. Enhancement errata add features or changes that can alter behavior and so should be tested before production deployment. A common filtering approach is to include only security and bugfix errata in production Content Views while deferring enhancements to a later, tested version. For example, create an errata filter that includes security and bugfix types, then publish a Content View version named to indicate the policy. A misconception is that security errata never cause regressions; while rare, security patches can sometimes change behavior, so always test critical updates. The practical effect of an errata filter is that the dnf updateinfo lists on clients will reflect only the allowed categories. Your checklist: build the filter, publish a new CV version, promote it, and then verify on a client using dnf updateinfo list security and list enhancement to confirm the expected visibility. Errata Types and Errata Filters means errata filters let you allow or block updates by type, enabling policies such as production-only security and bugfix updates.. In practical terms, security, bugfix, enhancement — how to include or exclude each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Errata filter rule
keyIdea.text: Errata filters let you allow or block updates by type, enabling policies such as production-only security and bugfix updates.

content.html:
Core Concept › Errata Types
Security
Critical for vulnerabilities
Prioritize testing and deployment. Often allowed for rapid promotion to production after verification.
Bugfix
Stability fixes
Important for system reliability; typically promoted after QA validation.
Enhancement
Feature changes
Defer to non-production until tested. Enhancements can change behavior and should be released cautiously.
Example filter
hammer content-view filter create --content-view "RHEL8_Base_CV" \
  --name "Security_Bugfix_Only" \
  --type erratum \
  --inclusion-type include \
  --errata-type security,bugfix
This ensures published Content View versions only include the listed errata types.
Verification
On a registered client run dnf updateinfo list security and list enhancement to confirm the filter's effect.
Key Takeaway

Errata filters implement policy at publish time — include only the categories you trust for each lifecycle stage.

screens.title: Module Stream Filters (RHEL 8+)
screens.narratorSegment: Module streams in RHEL 8 and later allow multiple major versions of a component to coexist, such as different Python or Node. js streams. A module stream filter ensures a specific stream is enabled across your Content View, which prevents clients from unexpectedly consuming another version. Use this when your applications require a consistent ABI or runtime. For example, enable the python38 stream in the AppStream repository to guarantee Python three.8 packages are included. A common error is leaving module streams unset and then seeing different hosts pull different streams from AppStream, leading to subtle behavior differences. When creating module filters, list the repository and stream explicitly so the Content View includes the desired artifacts. As with other filters, publish a new Content View version after enabling a module stream. The concrete benefit is reproducibility: every host that uses the promoted Content View will see the same module stream choices, which reduces the chance of runtime incompatibilities in production. Module Stream Filters (RHEL 8+) means module stream filters pin which stream of a component is available in a content view, ensuring runtime consistency.. In practical terms, ensuring consistent module stream selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Module streams
keyIdea.text: Module stream filters pin which stream of a component is available in a Content View, ensuring runtime consistency.

content.html:
Definition › Module Stream Filter
What is a module stream?
A stream is a distinct minor/major line of packages for a component, allowing multiple versions to be available in parallel.
Why pin a stream?
To ensure all hosts use the same runtime version and avoid runtime incompatibilities caused by drifting streams.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly enable module streams in Content Views to guarantee consistent component versions across lifecycle environments.

Example
hammer content-view filter create --content-view "RHEL8_Base_CV" \
  --name "Enable_Python38" \
  --type module \
  --inclusion-type include \
  --module-stream "python38" \
  --repository "Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 for x86_64 - AppStream RPMs"
Publish a new Content View version after creating this filter to include the module stream.
Pitfall
Not specifying streams can let hosts pick differing streams from AppStream; always pin in production-focused Content Views.

screens.title: Publishing Filters and Content View Versions
screens.narratorSegment: Filters take effect only when you publish a new Content View version. The publish action captures the curated content set and creates an immutable snapshot. Best practice is to name versions clearly and include a description of the filters applied. A typical flow is: create or edit filters; validate in the UI or via hammer; publish a new version with an informative description; and then promote that version sequentially through your lifecycle environments. Automation is valuable here: scripting publish and promotion with hammer or the A P I reduces manual error and ensures traceability. A common pitfall is publishing without testing in a Development environment. Always publish to Development first, run client checks, then promote to QA and Production after validation. If you later change filter rules, you must publish another version because published versions are immutable. The concrete example: after creating an errata filter that includes security and bugfix errata, run hammer to publish a new version and tag it like v1.2.0. The takeaway: treat publishing as a release step with the same controls and documentation you give to application releases.

content.html:
Process › Publishing & Promotion
Publish checklist
  1. Create or update filters.
  2. Validate in Development repository.
  3. Publish a new Content View version with a clear description.
  4. Promote sequentially: Dev → QA → Prod.
Automation tip
Automate publishing and promotion with hammer or the API to ensure consistent naming and reduce manual steps during patch cycles.
Key Takeaway

Treat publishing like a release: validate, document, and promote immutable versions in a controlled sequence.

Example command
# Publish a new Content View version (example)
hammer content-view publish --name "RHEL8_Sec_Bugfix_CustomApp" \
  --description "v1.2.0 - RHEL 8 with security and bugfix errata and custom app"
Follow with promotion commands for each lifecycle environment.
Misconception
You cannot change a published Content View version; edits require publishing a new version.

screens.title: Effective Errata Management
screens.narratorSegment: Errata management is more than running updates; it is about intent and scope. Security errata fix vulnerabilities and should often be treated as high priority. Bugfix errata resolve defects and are usually important for stability. Enhancement errata introduce new capabilities and can change behavior, so they should be staged and tested. Best practice is to control errata exposure through Content View filters and promotion, not by applying everything in place. When applying errata, target hosts, host groups, or lifecycle environments that are appropriate for the risk level. Use Satellite's remote execution capabilities to apply specific errata IDs to a host when an emergency fix is required. A common mistake is bulk-applying all errata without considering enhancements, which can destabilize systems. Example commands include listing applicable errata for a host with hammer, and applying a specific erratum by ID. The takeaway: use filters and staged promotion to make errata application predictable and auditable, and adopt a rollback plan when applying large or risky updates. Effective Errata Management means prioritize security and bugfix errata, defer enhancements for testing, and target errata application to appropriate hosts or groups.. In practical terms, categorize, prioritize, and target errata carefully. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Errata practice
keyIdea.text: Prioritize security and bugfix errata, defer enhancements for testing, and target errata application to appropriate hosts or groups.

content.html:
Core Concept › Errata Management
Categorize and prioritize
Treat security errata as urgent, bugfixes as important, and enhancements as deferred until tested. Use filters to enforce these categories by environment.
Targeted application
Apply errata to specific hosts or host groups when necessary. Avoid broad, untested rollouts in production.
Key Takeaway

Errata should be applied deliberately: filter, publish, test, then promote and apply to the intended hosts.

Example commands
# List applicable errata for a host
hammer host erratum list --name myclient.example.com --organization "MyOrg"

# Apply a specific erratum to a host
hammer host erratum apply --host myclient.example.com --errata-ids RHSA-2023:1234 --organization "MyOrg"
Use these cautiously and document the change for traceability.
Misconception
Applying all errata is not always safer. Enhancements may introduce regressions; use filtering to prevent untested features from reaching production.

screens.title: Applying Errata to Hosts
screens.narratorSegment: Applying errata is an operation with scope and consequence. You can target a single host, a host group, or all hosts in a lifecycle environment. Choose the scope based on the risk and required windows for testing. If a single host exhibits a vulnerability or bug, apply only the required erratum to that host and monitor. For wide security issues, publish a tested Content View version with the required errata included, promote it, and then apply updates during a maintenance window. A practical command flow is to list applicable errata for a host using hammer, inspect the erratum ID, and apply that specific erratum. Always prefer applying errata by ID rather than a blanket update to avoid bringing in enhancements unexpectedly. A misconception is that remote execution eliminates the need for checks; remote execution simplifies delivery, but you still must verify preconditions like subscriptions and correct CV registration. The takeaway: choose the correct scope, validate the erratum content, and have a rollback or remediation plan before broad application. Applying Errata to Hosts means apply errata with precise scope and validate host registration, subscription, and lifecycle environment before execution.. In practical terms, target hosts, host groups, and lifecycle environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Apply errata with precise scope and validate host registration, subscription, and lifecycle environment before execution.

content.html:
Process › Applying Errata
Scope selection
Decide whether to apply to a single host, a host group, or an entire lifecycle environment based on risk and testing results.
Execution safety
Confirm subscriptions, host registration, and Content View promotion before running remote execution to apply updates.
Key Takeaway

Prefer targeted errata application and validate host state. Use remote execution with caution and monitoring.

Example commands
# List errata for a host
hammer host erratum list --name myclient.example.com --organization "MyOrg"

# Apply a specific erratum to a host
hammer host erratum apply --host myclient.example.com --errata-ids RHSA-2023:1234 --organization "MyOrg"
Prefer applying specific IDs during targeted maintenance windows.
Misconception
Remote execution is not a substitute for validation. It simplifies deployment but you still need pre-checks and post-verification steps.

screens.title: Integrating Custom RPMs and Repositories
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite is a convenient distribution point for your custom RPMs. The typical pattern is to create a custom product, add a yum repository, and upload RPMs either through the UI or with hammer and repository upload-content. For automated builds, configure the repository to sync from an internal web server or artifact storage. When adding a custom RPM repository to a Content View, include it alongside the RHEL BaseOS and AppStream repos so clients get both vendor and in-house packages from the same Content View. A pitfall is forgetting to publish a new Content View version after uploading RPMs; the new package will not be visible to clients until you publish and promote. Example flow: create product, create repository, upload RPMs, create Content View including the repo, publish, and promote. The key benefit is control: you can ensure internal packages are scanned, versioned, and distributed in your lifecycle just like vendor content. Always test installation from a registered client before broad promotion. Integrating Custom RPMs and Repositories means create a product and repo, upload or sync rpms, include them in a content view, publish and promote to distribute internally.. In practical terms, upload, automate, and distribute internal packages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Custom RPMs
Create and upload
Create a custom product and yum repository in Satellite, then upload RPMs via UI or hammer repository upload-content for automation.
Include in Content View
Add your custom repo to the Content View alongside RHEL repos so clients can install both vendor and internal packages.
Key Takeaway

Treat custom RPMs as first-class content: upload, publish, and promote them within Content Views for reproducible deployments.

Hands-on example
Create a product and repository, upload your my-custom-app RPM, add the repo to a Content View, publish, and verify installation with sudo dnf install my-custom-app on a registered client.
Pitfall
Forgetting to publish a new Content View version after uploading RPMs prevents clients from seeing the content.

screens.title: Custom ISOs and Container Images
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite supports distributing files and container images in addition to RPMs. For custom ISOs, create a "File" type repository within a product and upload the ISO; these files can then be referenced by provisioning templates or made available to teams. For container images, Satellite implements an OCI-compliant registry. You can create a Docker type repository in a product to define the namespace, then push images using podman after authenticating to Satellite's registry. A standard workflow: podman login to satellite. example. com:8443, tag your image with the product namespace, and podman push. This makes images available to internal clusters and can enable vulnerability scanning and air-gapped distribution. A common misconception is that container images must be synchronized from external registries; while Satellite can sync external registries, pushing images is appropriate for developer-built artifacts. The architecture benefit is centralization: Satellite becomes your secure registry and file store for provisioning and distribution. Always verify access by pulling the pushed image from a client or cluster before relying on it in production. Custom ISOs and Container Images means use file repositories for isos and the docker repo type plus podman push for internal container images; confirm pulls from clients.. In practical terms, file repositories and satellite's integrated oci registry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture › ISOs & Container Images
Custom ISOs
Create a File type repository and upload ISOs. Use them in provisioning templates for consistent installations and utilities.
Container images
Create a Docker type repository and push images into Satellite's registry to centralize distribution and scanning.
Key Takeaway

Use Satellite's file and OCI support to centralize internal ISOs and images, and verify pulls from your clusters or clients.

Podman push example
# Login to Satellite registry
podman login -u admin -p <admin_password> satellite.example.com:8443

# Tag the image
podman tag my-custom-app:latest satellite.example.com:8443/my-custom-product/my-custom-app:latest

# Push the image
podman push satellite.example.com:8443/my-custom-product/my-custom-app:latest
After pushing, confirm the image can be pulled by your internal clusters.
Misconception
Pushing custom images is not the same as syncing from external registries. Use push for internal builds and sync for third-party registries.

screens.title: Content View Versioning and Promotion
screens.narratorSegment: Content View versioning is built around immutability. Once you publish a version, its content cannot be changed. This ensures what was tested in Development is what reaches Production when promoted. Follow a sequential promotion model: Library or Library-derived versions to Development, then QA, then Production. Use clear naming and descriptive comments for each published version so teams know what is included and why. For example, include entries like "v1.2.3 - RHEL 8 with latest security errata and custom app update" to make rollbacks and audits straightforward. Automate publishing and promotion where possible to reduce manual errors; hammer and the A P I support these workflows. A common misconception is that immutability limits agility — instead, it enables reliable rollouts because any change requires a deliberate new version, encouraging testing and traceability. The bottom line: design a promotion pipeline that mirrors your test gating and keep versions descriptive and auditable. Content View Versioning and Promotion means published content view versions are immutable; promote them sequentially and use clear naming for traceability.. In practical terms, immutability, naming, and sequential promotion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Version immutability
keyIdea.text: Published Content View versions are immutable; promote them sequentially and use clear naming for traceability.

content.html:
Best Practice › Versioning & Promotion
Step 1 — Publish
Capture the curated Content View into an immutable version with a clear description.
Step 2 — Test in Development
Validate packages, errata, and custom RPMs on registered clients in Development.
Step 3 — Promote sequentially
After verification promote to QA then Production. Automate where possible for consistency.
Naming guideline
Include version, platform, and filter summary, e.g., "v1.2.3 - RHEL8 - security+bugfix + my-app" for clear audit trails.
Key Takeaway
Immutability ensures reproducibility. Publish intentionally, test thoroughly, and use sequential promotion to reduce risk.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Content View Synchronization and Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: When content doesn't appear where you expect, follow a checklist of common causes. First, verify the underlying repository has been synchronized; an out-of-date repo means the Content View cannot include the content. Second, check Content View filters — ensure the filter is not excluding the package or erratum. Third, confirm the Content View version containing the content has been published and promoted to the lifecycle environment the host is registered to. Fourth, examine host registration and subscription status; a client must be registered to the correct Content View/Lifecycle Environment and have valid subscriptions. For synchronization failures, check Satellite logs such as /var/log/messages and /var/log/foreman/production. log and verify network connectivity to the Red Hat CDN or external sources, as well as disk space on /var/lib/pulp. A common misconception is to blame the client first; often the server-side publish or promotion step was missed. The practical diagnostic flow is: repo sync status, filter rules, published versions, lifecycle promotion, host registration, and then logs. Keep backups and document fixes for recurring issues. Troubleshooting Content View Synchronization and Visibility means verify repo sync, filter rules, published versions, promotion state, host registration, and server logs to diagnose missing content.. In practical terms, checks, logs, and common fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify repo sync, filter rules, published versions, promotion state, host registration, and server logs to diagnose missing content.

content.html:
Troubleshooting › Sync & Visibility
Diagnostic checklist
  • Confirm repository synchronization.
  • Verify Content View filters are not excluding content.
  • Ensure the correct Content View version is published and promoted.
  • Check host registration and subscriptions.
Log locations
Review /var/log/messages and /var/log/foreman/production.log for synchronization and API errors. Check disk space on /var/lib/pulp.
Key Takeaway

Work top-down: server sync and publish, filters and promotion, then client registration and logs. Document any repeated failures.

Practical fix example
If a package is missing, check if the repo contains it, ensure no filter excludes it, publish a new CV version, promote to the host's lifecycle environment, then on the host run dnf clean all and retry.
Misconception
Don't assume the client is the issue first; often a missing publish or promotion is the root cause.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's lock in three short, practical concepts you can use daily. First, Package Filter: filter by package name and version to exclude known-bad RPMs while allowing other updates. Second, Errata Filter: configure errata inclusion by type—security, bugfix, enhancement—to enforce environment policies and reduce unexpected behavior. Third, Module Stream Filter: explicitly enable module streams for RHEL 8+ to guarantee consistent runtimes across hosts. Each of these filters affects what is included at publish time, so publish a new Content View version whenever you change filters. Treat published versions as immutable, promote them sequentially through your lifecycle, and automate publishing and promotion where possible. These three core ideas help you curate content safely, apply updates deliberately, and keep production systems stable. Which filter will you apply first in your environment? A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical mental model for controlling exactly what content reaches hosts through Red Hat Satellite. You will learn how Content View filters let you include or exclude packages, errata types, and module streams; how to manage errata carefully so production systems stay secure and stable; and how to integrate custom RPMs, ISOs, and container images into Satellite for internal distribution. I'll give concrete CLI examples you can reuse, plus a hands-on lab that practices errata filtering and custom RPM upload. We'll also cover Content View versioning and promotion best practices so you can roll changes forward safely, and show key troubleshooting checks when content doesn't appear. This matters because uncontrolled updates or untested enhancements are a common source of outages. By the end you'll be able to design a Content View that enforces security policies, distributes internal packages, and promotes versions through a lifecycle in a predictable, auditable way. As you follow the visuals, notice the three core themes: curate, verify, and promote. Which of those will be most important for your environment?

These objectives target the skills you'll use immediately when operating Satellite. First, you'll implement advanced Content View filters that select packages by name, version, errata type, or module stream so only approved content reaches each lifecycle stage. Second, you'll manage errata intentionally: prioritize security and bugfix updates, defer enhancements, and apply updates to hosts or host groups with minimal disruption. Third, you'll integrate custom content—uploading RPMs and ISOs and pushing container images to Satellite's registry—so internal artifacts are distributed securely. Fourth, you'll author and publish immutable Content View versions and promote them through a controlled lifecycle while troubleshooting common synchronization issues. Each objective connects to real tasks: creating a filter with hammer, applying a targeted erratum to a host, uploading an internal RPM repository, and diagnosing why a client does not see a published version. These skills reduce risk, increase reproducibility, and make audits simpler. Practice in a Development environment before applying to Production, and use the verified competency milestones to measure readiness.

This second objective panel expands the practical skills to apply once your filters and content are defined. You'll learn to use the hammer CLI and Satellite UI to create filters and check applicable errata for a host. You'll practice uploading custom RPMs to a product repository and synchronizing content, and you'll use podman commands to push container images to Satellite's integrated registry. The aim is repeatability: name and describe Content View versions clearly, automate publishing and promotion where possible, and confirm clients are registered to the correct lifecycle environment. A useful test is to register a client to your Development Content View and compare the dnf updateinfo lists for security, bugfix, and enhancement errata. If you cannot see expected content, the checklist in this lesson guides you through verifying repo sync, filters, published versions, host registration, and subscription status. This objective emphasizes safe automation and a measured rollback plan for production.

A Content View filter is a rule set that narrows the content included in a Content View before publishing. Filters can target package names and versions, errata types or IDs, and module streams. The core idea is curation: decide ahead of publishing what is eligible for testing and promotion. For example, if a particular package version causes instability, you can create a package filter that excludes that version so it never reaches your environments. Or, if your policy requires only security and bugfix updates in production, an errata filter that includes only those types enforces that rule consistently. A common misconception is that filters are reversible on a published version. They are not: filters affect what is included when you publish. Changing filters requires publishing a new Content View version. A concrete example: use hammer to create an errata filter named "Security_Bugfix_Only" and include only the security and bugfix types. After publishing, promote that version through your lifecycle. The key takeaway is that filters are preventive controls that enforce policy at publish time; treat them as part of your pipeline, test in lower environments, and document each filter's purpose with clear names and descriptions.

Filtering by package name and version is a precise way to prevent a known-bad RPM from entering your lifecycle. Define an exclusion filter specifying both the package name and the offending version. This is often used when a vendor update regresses functionality or when compliance requires a fixed package version. A practical example: you discover that bad-package version 1.0.0 causes a service crash on all controllers. Create a Content View filter that excludes package "bad-package" version "1.0.0" and attach it to the Content View containing your RHEL 8 repositories. Remember filters are evaluated before publishing, so after creating the filter you must publish a new Content View version and promote it. A common mistake is excluding too broadly, for example excluding a package by name without scoping the version, which may block required updates. Another pitfall is not documenting the filter rationale. In practice, include the filter name and description that reference the bug tracking ID or incident number. The takeaway: prefer targeted exclusions, publish new versions, and test in Development before promoting to Production. Package Name and Version Filters means target package name plus version to exclude known-bad rpms while preserving healthy updates.. In practical terms, precise exclusion or inclusion of problematic rpms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Errata in Satellite are categorized as security, bugfix, or enhancement. Each type represents different risk and priority. Security errata fix vulnerabilities and should be prioritized for most environments. Bugfix errata correct defects and typically improve stability. Enhancement errata add features or changes that can alter behavior and so should be tested before production deployment. A common filtering approach is to include only security and bugfix errata in production Content Views while deferring enhancements to a later, tested version. For example, create an errata filter that includes security and bugfix types, then publish a Content View version named to indicate the policy. A misconception is that security errata never cause regressions; while rare, security patches can sometimes change behavior, so always test critical updates. The practical effect of an errata filter is that the dnf updateinfo lists on clients will reflect only the allowed categories. Your checklist: build the filter, publish a new CV version, promote it, and then verify on a client using dnf updateinfo list security and list enhancement to confirm the expected visibility. Errata Types and Errata Filters means errata filters let you allow or block updates by type, enabling policies such as production-only security and bugfix updates.. In practical terms, security, bugfix, enhancement — how to include or exclude each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module streams in RHEL 8 and later allow multiple major versions of a component to coexist, such as different Python or Node. js streams. Filters take effect only when you publish a new Content View version. The publish action captures the curated content set and creates an immutable snapshot. Best practice is to name versions clearly and include a description of the filters applied. A typical flow is: create or edit filters; validate in the UI or via hammer; publish a new version with an informative description; and then promote that version sequentially through your lifecycle environments. Automation is valuable here: scripting publish and promotion with hammer or the A P I reduces manual error and ensures traceability. A common pitfall is publishing without testing in a Development environment. Always publish to Development first, run client checks, then promote to QA and Production after validation. If you later change filter rules, you must publish another version because published versions are immutable. Errata management is more than running updates; it is about intent and scope. Security errata fix vulnerabilities and should often be treated as high priority. Best practice is to control errata exposure through Content View filters and promotion, not by applying everything in place. When applying errata, target hosts, host groups, or lifecycle environments that are appropriate for the risk level. Content View versioning is built around immutability. Once you publish a version, its content cannot be changed. This ensures what was tested in Development is what reaches Production when promoted. Follow a sequential promotion model: Library or Library-derived versions to Development, then QA, then Production. When content doesn't appear where you expect, follow a checklist of common causes. First, verify the underlying repository has been synchronized; an out-of-date repo means the Content View cannot include the content. Second, check Content View filters — ensure the filter is not excluding the package or erratum. Third, confirm the Content View version containing the content has been published and promoted to the lifecycle environment the host is registered to. Fourth, examine host registration and subscription status; a client must be registered to the correct Content View/Lifecycle Environment and have valid subscriptions.
